subject: chemistry

items.q: A reaction transfers energy to the surroundings. What must be true of the product molecules?
items.correct: They have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred out.
items.misconception: They have more energy than the reactants, by the amount given out.
items.why: Released energy is read as gained energy, and exothermic reactions are associated with heat and flames, so students picture the products as the energy-rich end of the change. The energy given out has to come from somewhere, and it comes from the chemicals, so the products must sit lower in energy by exactly that amount.
items.random_wrong: They have less energy, and the energy released no longer exists.

items.q: Which statement about energy during a chemical reaction is correct?
items.correct: The total energy in the universe is the same after the reaction as before.
items.misconception: Energy is conserved only in reactions that give energy out to the surroundings.
items.why: Conserved is heard as unchanged and then applied to each part separately, so students conclude that nothing can move between the chemicals and the surroundings. Conservation is about the total, not about each part. Energy moves freely between chemicals and surroundings while the total stays fixed.
items.random_wrong: Some of the energy is destroyed as the surroundings are being warmed.

items.q: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?
items.correct: It transfers energy to the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
items.misconception: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
items.why: In everyday life things get hot because you heat them: a kettle, an oven, a radiator. Students carry that pattern across and assume the hot object is the one receiving energy, which reverses the two words. Ask which way energy moves relative to the surroundings. Exothermic sends energy out to the surroundings, and the thermometer is measuring the surroundings, so a rise means energy came out.
items.random_wrong: It transfers energy out, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.

items.q: Which of these reactions is exothermic?
items.correct: the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali
items.misconception: the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
items.why: The presence of heat is read as evidence of heat being produced, and the constant supply from the Bunsen makes it look as though the reaction is the source. Ask what happens if the flame is removed: the reaction stops, because it depends on energy being supplied. That is what endothermic means.
items.random_wrong: the reaction inside a sports injury cold pack

items.q: Magnesium ribbon is lit with a Bunsen flame and burns brightly, warming the tripod above it. Why is this reaction described as exothermic?
items.correct: Combustion transfers energy to the surroundings, and that is why the tripod warms.
items.misconception: Energy had to be supplied by the flame, so energy is taken in overall here.
items.why: Students merge starting a reaction with the overall energy change, so any reaction that needs heating is filed as endothermic. Separate the start from the balance sheet. The energy needed to begin a reaction is the activation energy; the overall change is judged by whether the surroundings end up warmer or cooler.
items.random_wrong: The oxidation takes in energy from the surrounding air, making it glow.

items.q: A hand warmer contains iron powder that oxidises slowly once the pack is opened. Why does the pack become warm?
items.correct: The oxidation is exothermic and transfers energy to your hands and the air.
items.misconception: The pack takes energy in from your own hand, and this is what makes it warm.
items.why: Students know that heat flows between hand and object and pick the wrong direction, because taking in energy is loosely linked with anything to do with warmth. If energy flowed from your hand into the pack, your hand would feel colder. It feels warmer, so the pack is the source and the reaction is exothermic.
items.random_wrong: The reaction is endothermic, so it lets out the heat it had stored.

items.q: Which statement describes an endothermic reaction?
items.correct: It takes energy in from the surroundings, so their temperature falls.
items.misconception: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature will rise.
items.why: In everyday life things get hot because you heat them: a kettle, an oven, a radiator. Students carry that pattern across and assume the hot object is the one receiving energy, which reverses the two words. Ask which way energy moves relative to the surroundings. Exothermic sends energy out to the surroundings, and the thermometer is measuring the surroundings, so a rise means energy came out.
items.random_wrong: It gives out energy, and so the temperature of the surroundings falls.

items.q: Copper carbonate is heated strongly and breaks down into copper oxide and carbon dioxide. Why is this reaction endothermic?
items.correct: Energy is taken in to break the compound down.
items.misconception: Energy is given out because a hot flame is used here.
items.why: The presence of heat is read as evidence of heat being produced, and the constant supply from the Bunsen makes it look as though the reaction is the source. Ask what happens if the flame is removed: the reaction stops, because it depends on energy being supplied. That is what endothermic means.
items.random_wrong: Energy is stored, then released as the gas escapes.

items.q: Citric acid solution is stirred with sodium hydrogencarbonate. The mixture fizzes and the thermometer falls from 21 °C to 15 °C. What does this show?
items.correct: The reaction is endothermic and takes energy in from the surroundings.
items.misconception: The reaction is exothermic, as the fizzing shows energy leaving.
items.why: Vigorous bubbling looks energetic, and students equate visible activity with energy being given out to the surroundings. Judge the direction from the thermometer, not from how lively the reaction looks. Here the reading falls, so energy has been taken in.
items.random_wrong: The reaction is exothermic, since the chemicals have lost energy.

items.q: A student measures the temperature of the surroundings before and after four reactions. Which result shows an endothermic reaction?
items.correct: The temperature fell from 22.0 °C to 16.5 °C during the reaction.
items.misconception: The temperature rose from 22.0 °C to 31.5 °C during this reaction.
items.why: In everyday life things get hot because you heat them: a kettle, an oven, a radiator. Students carry that pattern across and assume the hot object is the one receiving energy, which reverses the two words. Ask which way energy moves relative to the surroundings. Exothermic sends energy out to the surroundings, and the thermometer is measuring the surroundings, so a rise means energy came out.
items.random_wrong: The temperature rose from 16.5 °C to 22.0 °C as it went along.

items.q: During a neutralisation the thermometer in the mixture rises by 8 °C. What has happened to the energy?
items.correct: It has been transferred from the chemicals to the surroundings.
items.misconception: It has been transferred from the surroundings and into the chemicals.
items.why: Students see the reading go up and attribute the gain to the reaction rather than to the surroundings that the thermometer is actually in. The thermometer reads the surroundings. Surroundings up means chemicals down, and the reaction is exothermic.
items.random_wrong: It has been created by the acid and alkali as they react together.

items.q: A sports injury pack and a hand warmer each rely on a chemical reaction. Which comparison is correct?
items.correct: The injury pack is endothermic and the warmer exothermic.
items.misconception: The injury pack is exothermic; the hand warmer is endothermic.
items.why: Heat treatment for aching muscles is familiar, so students assume every sports pack is meant to warm rather than cool. The specification pairs injury packs with endothermic reactions. A fresh injury is cooled, and cooling means energy is taken from the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: Both are exothermic, but the injury pack releases energy slowly.

items.q: A self-heating can warms coffee using the reaction of calcium oxide with water. Which property makes this reaction suitable for that use?
items.correct: It is exothermic, so it transfers enough energy to warm the drink in the can.
items.misconception: It is endothermic, so it draws energy out of the air and into the drink.
items.why: Endo sounds like it should mean giving out, and students remember only that the device gets hot, not which way energy moves. Endothermic means energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool. Anything designed to warm something must use an exothermic reaction.
items.random_wrong: It is exothermic, so the reacting chemicals themselves become hotter.

items.q: In Required practical 4 a student adds different volumes of sodium hydroxide to 25 cm3 of acid and records the highest temperature reached. What is the independent variable?
items.correct: the volume of sodium hydroxide added
items.misconception: the highest temperature that is reached
items.why: Students pick the variable they care about most, or the one written first in the results table, rather than the one they set themselves. The independent variable is the one you choose and change; the dependent variable is the one you measure as a result. Here you set the volume and read the temperature.
items.random_wrong: the concentration of the acid used

items.q: Why is the reacting mixture in Required practical 4 placed in a polystyrene cup with a lid?
items.correct: to reduce the energy transferred to and from the surroundings
items.misconception: to hold the mixture at a steady temperature all through the reaction
items.why: Any piece of apparatus is assumed to be there to make the reaction work better, and insulation is not recognised as being about the accuracy of the measurement. The cup does not touch the chemistry; it insulates. Its job is to stop energy leaking to the bench and the air so the reading reflects the reaction.
items.random_wrong: to make the reaction go faster so that a change can be seen sooner

items.q: Two reactant particles collide with each other but no reaction takes place. What is the reason?
items.correct: They collided with too little energy to react.
items.misconception: Every collision must react, so this cannot happen.
items.why: Collision theory is remembered as particles must collide, and the second condition about sufficient energy is dropped. The specification requires both conditions: particles must collide with each other and with sufficient energy. A gentle collision simply bounces apart.
items.random_wrong: They collided with less than the energy given out here.

items.q: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?
items.correct: the minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react
items.misconception: the energy that the product molecules are left with at the very end
items.why: Students measure heights from the axis out of habit with graphs, rather than from the reactants line where the reaction starts. The activation energy is a difference, not a height above zero: measure from the reactants up to the peak.
items.random_wrong: the total amount of energy the reaction gives out overall

items.q: Which set of quantities can be shown on a reaction profile?
items.correct: the relative energies of the reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change
items.misconception: the relative energies of the reactants and the products and the time that the whole reaction takes to finish
items.why: Students judge by how impressive the change looks rather than by its direction, so small rises are dismissed as experimental error. The direction of the change decides exothermic or endothermic; the size only tells you how much energy was transferred.
items.random_wrong: the activation energy on its own, because the products are not marked anywhere on the diagram

items.q: A student draws a reaction profile for an endothermic reaction. Which description of the drawing is correct?
items.correct: The products line lies above the reactants, joined by a curved peak.
items.misconception: The products line lies below the reactants, joined by a curve with a peak.
items.why: Higher on the diagram is read as more energy released, so students draw the bigger arrow upwards instead of tracking where the energy ends up. Height on the profile is the energy of the chemicals. Energy transferred out of the chemicals leaves the products lower down.
items.random_wrong: A straight sloping line runs from the reactants line up to the products.

items.q: A reaction profile shows the products at a lower energy than the reactants. What does this tell you about the reaction?
items.correct: It is exothermic and gives out energy.
items.misconception: It is endothermic and takes in energy overall.
items.why: Higher on the diagram is read as more energy released, so students draw the bigger arrow upwards instead of tracking where the energy ends up. Height on the profile is the energy of the chemicals. Energy transferred out of the chemicals leaves the products lower down.
items.random_wrong: It is exothermic only if the peak is low.

items.q: Why must colliding particles have at least the activation energy?
items.correct: because it is the energy that is needed for the reaction to occur
items.misconception: because it is the energy the reaction gives to the surroundings
items.why: Both quantities are marked on the same reaction profile, and students read whichever arrow they meet first without checking what it joins. The activation energy runs from the reactants up to the peak; the overall energy change runs from the reactants across to the products. Different arrows, different meanings.
items.random_wrong: because it is only needed when a reaction is endothermic

items.q: During a chemical reaction, what happens to the bonds in the reactants?
items.correct: Energy must be supplied so that they break.
items.misconception: Energy is released as each one of them breaks.
items.why: Everyday breaking is destructive and seems to let something out, and students imagine energy stored in the bond like a compressed spring. A bond is an attraction that must be pulled apart, and pulling anything apart against attraction costs energy. Breaking takes in, making gives out.
items.random_wrong: They break with no energy change at all.

items.q: What happens to energy when the bonds in the products are formed?
items.correct: Energy is released as these bonds form.
items.misconception: Energy is released only if it is exothermic.
items.why: Exothermic is linked with lots of energy, and the breaking term is the one students meet first, so it is assumed to be the larger of the two. Whichever term is larger decides the direction. More energy out on making than in on breaking leaves a surplus that goes to the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: Energy must be supplied to make them form.

items.q: A student is given a table of bond energies for a reaction. What can these values be used to calculate?
items.correct: the energy taken in breaking bonds and released forming them
items.misconception: the total energy of the reaction, by adding up every value in the table
items.why: Addition feels safer than subtraction, and students lose track of which bonds belong to the reactants and which to the products. Make two sums: one for bonds broken and one for bonds formed. The overall energy change is the difference between them.
items.random_wrong: the number of bonds broken and the number of bonds formed in total

items.q: How is the overall energy change of a reaction found from bond energies?
items.correct: the sum of the energy needed to break bonds minus the sum released forming bonds
items.misconception: the sum of the energy released forming bonds minus the sum needed to break
items.why: The subtraction is remembered as products minus reactants from other calculations, so students take the sums in the wrong order. Work in the order the reaction happens: break first, make second. Break minus make gives a negative answer for an exothermic reaction.
items.random_wrong: the sum of the energy needed to break bonds added to the sum released

items.q: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is the overall energy change?
items.correct: -184 kJ/mol, so this is exothermic
items.misconception: +1540 kJ/mol, adding all the values up
items.why: Addition feels safer than subtraction, and students lose track of which bonds belong to the reactants and which to the products. Make two sums: one for bonds broken and one for bonds formed. The overall energy change is the difference between them.
items.random_wrong: +184 kJ/mol, so it is endothermic

items.q: In an exothermic reaction, how do the two bond energy sums compare?
items.correct: Forming new bonds releases more than breaking bonds needs.
items.misconception: Breaking existing bonds needs more than forming new bonds gives out.
items.why: Exothermic is linked with lots of energy, and the breaking term is the one students meet first, so it is assumed to be the larger of the two. Whichever term is larger decides the direction. More energy out on making than in on breaking leaves a surplus that goes to the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: More bonds are formed in the products than are broken overall.

items.q: A reaction is endothermic. What does this tell you about the bond energy sums?
items.correct: Breaking bonds needs more than forming lets out.
items.misconception: More bonds are broken than are formed in this reaction.
items.why: Counting bonds is easier than adding bond energies, so students balance the tally and assume the energies must balance too. Different bonds have different bond energies. Four strong bonds formed can release far more than four weak bonds needed to break.
items.random_wrong: Forming bonds gives out more than breaking needs.

items.q: A neutralisation warms the solution in the beaker. Have the surroundings warmed up?
items.correct: Yes. The solvent, the beaker and the air around the reacting chemicals are all the surroundings, so the solution warming up is the surroundings warming up.
items.misconception: The surroundings means the room, so warming of the solution itself does not count as energy transferred to the surroundings.
items.why: The word surroundings sounds like the space around the apparatus, so students exclude the water the chemicals are dissolved in, even though that is what the thermometer sits in. Define the system as the reacting chemicals only. Everything else, starting with the solvent, is the surroundings, which is why a thermometer in the mixture measures the surroundings.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In an exothermic reaction, what has happened to the energy that was released?
items.correct: It has been transferred to the surroundings, warming them. The total energy in the universe is unchanged.
items.misconception: The energy is used up or destroyed by the reaction.
items.why: Students hear energy is lost as heat and take lost literally, so the energy leaves the accounts altogether instead of appearing in the surroundings. Track where the energy has gone rather than whether it has gone. Energy is conserved: what leaves the chemicals arrives in the surroundings and can be measured as a temperature rise.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does conservation of energy mean the reactants and products have the same energy?
items.correct: No. Conservation applies to the universe as a whole; the products can be lower in energy provided the difference has gone to the surroundings.
items.misconception: Energy must balance on each side of the equation, so reactants and products have equal energy.
items.why: Students transfer the rule they learned for conservation of mass, where both sides of a balanced equation carry the same atoms, onto energy without including the surroundings in the balance. Include the surroundings in the accounts. Chemicals plus surroundings is constant; chemicals alone are not.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the temperature when hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide?
items.correct: It rises. Neutralisation is exothermic and transfers energy to the surroundings.
items.misconception: Neutralisation cancels the acid and the alkali out, so there is no energy change and no temperature change.
items.why: The word neutral suggests nothing happening, and students picture the acid and alkali destroying each other rather than reacting to make a salt and water. Neutralisation is a chemical reaction that makes new substances, and it is one of the exothermic reactions named by the specification.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Iron powder rusting inside a hand warmer is a slow reaction. Does it still transfer energy?
items.correct: Yes. Oxidation of iron is exothermic, and the pack becomes noticeably warm.
items.misconception: Slow reactions with no flame transfer no energy to the surroundings.
items.why: Exothermic is associated with flames and explosions, so a quiet reaction with nothing to see is assumed to have no energy change. The specification lists many oxidation reactions as exothermic. Rate and energy change are separate: a slow reaction releases the same energy, just more gradually.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the energy go in an exothermic reaction?
items.correct: Out of the chemicals into the surroundings, which is why the temperature of the surroundings increases.
items.misconception: It is stored inside the product molecules, which is why exothermic products are described as high in energy.
items.why: Students meet stored chemical energy and place the energy in the products, missing that an exothermic reaction leaves the products lower in energy than the reactants. The energy transferred out is no longer in the chemicals. Exothermic products are lower in energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred out.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an exothermic reaction have an activation energy?
items.correct: Yes. Every reaction has an activation energy, whether it gives out energy overall or takes it in.
items.misconception: Only endothermic reactions need an activation energy, since exothermic reactions give energy out.
items.why: If a reaction releases energy, students assume it cannot also require any, so they treat the activation energy as belonging to endothermic changes alone. Bonds in the reactants must be broken in every reaction, so every reaction needs a minimum energy to start. Petrol still needs a spark.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What shape of line joins the reactants and products on a reaction profile?
items.correct: A curved line rising from the reactants over a peak and then falling to the products.
items.misconception: A straight sloping line drawn directly from the reactants to the products.
items.why: Students think of the diagram as a graph of two energy levels and join them with a ruler, leaving out the activation energy barrier entirely. The specification asks for a curved line showing the energy as the reaction proceeds, which must pass over the activation energy peak.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the energy when a bond in a product molecule is formed?
items.correct: Energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.
items.misconception: Energy has to be supplied to make new bonds, in the same way as for breaking them.
items.why: Making something sounds like work that must cost energy, so students apply the same sign to both processes and end up with no overall change. The two processes are opposite: breaking bonds takes energy in, forming bonds gives energy out. If both cost energy, no reaction could ever be exothermic.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, how much energy is released as the H-Cl bonds form?
items.correct: Two moles of H-Cl are formed, so it is 2 x 431 = 862 kJ, not 431 kJ.
items.misconception: Each bond energy in the table is used once, whatever the balancing numbers in the equation say.
items.why: The table gives one value per type of bond, so students treat it as a list of quantities to use once each and never go back to the balanced equation to count how many of each bond there actually are. List the bonds in every molecule first, using the balancing numbers, then multiply each bond energy by the number of that bond present.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions
